what: The stricter blind test run again with each house's height read from USGS 3DEP lidar, as the city pipeline reads it, and the house found in each photograph by the pipeline's open-vocabulary detector.
source: Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress), public domain; scans from the Library of Congress and its Wikimedia Commons mirror; building footprints (c) OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Photographs and drawings were deleted after scoring; only these numbers are kept. Heights: USGS 3D Elevation Program lidar (public domain), via the public Entwine tiles.
method: Given per house: one to three photographs (as many as the survey has of that front, at most three), the OpenStreetMap footprint, and the lidar. Nothing from the drawings.
Height: smc.lidar.region.building_height, unchanged -- the roof's 92nd percentile over the ground at the house's foot, from the newest 3DEP collection covering it (all seven are covered).
Width: the footprint's walls facing the survey's elevation, end to end.

Each photograph squared up from its own vanishing points; the house found as Grounding DINO boxes it (prompt 'house. building.', the most confident box across the frame's middle); its ground line is the box's foot, its ends the box's sides, and the lidar height laid up from the ground line at the squared-up photograph's own scale.

The pipeline unchanged: segmentation, detector, extract_front. Scored as before (centres within max(1.5 m, the opening's size), IoU >= 0.1), on the photograph the frontage filter would pick, with a fusion of all the house's photographs beside it.
A diagnostic run, not blind, gives the same photographs the drawing's own width and height, to tell how much of the loss is size and how much is finding the front and its openings.

findings: Lidar gets the height the photograph could not: within 6 per cent of the drawing at Larkin (7.34 m against 7.77), Carson (5.15 against 4.93) and J. S. Cain (6.97 against 7.34); 31-40 per cent over where a cupola, a tower or a tree rises above the drawn front (Banning 13.94 against 10.03, the Governor's Mansion 17.24 against 12.30, Stanford 17.97 against 13.71, Amesti 9.1 against 6.65). The first run's photograph-aspect heights were 2-4.6 times too tall.

But height was not what held the score down. With lidar heights, 16 of 113 drawn openings were found (43 per cent of predictions real), against 13 with heights from the photograph; and given the drawing's own width and height, still 16. The loss is in finding the front in an archival photograph and in the detector's proposals on it: about 31-37 openings proposed for 113 drawn, and the two large mansions (69 of the 113) yield 5-10 each.
Larkin, a plain two-storey front squarely photographed, holds in every blind run: 6 of 10 found, none false, 0.3-0.5 m position error.

On 2026-10-12 the same pipeline found 80 per cent of openings when the front was cut out of the photograph by hand. In the city that cut comes from the camera's recorded pose projected onto the footprint, not from finding the house in the picture, so that figure is the closer guide for the city -- where the pose is right; this test is the guide for photographs without a pose.
Fusing photographs still does worse than the filter's single photograph: the oblique views disagree with the square one.
